---
title: "Reconstruction"
---

`reconstruct_legal_provisions` builds a law's current text from nothing but its
DOF notes: it starts from the original publication and replays each reform
decree's own "se reforma, adiciona, deroga el artículo N ... para quedar como
sigue" instruction on top of it, article by article, filling back in, from the
article's own previous text, every fracción or inciso a reform elides with
"..." instead of repeating. It never reads anyone else's consolidated text of
the law.

```python
from nota2md import download_scjn_leyes_corpus, reconstruct_legal_provisions

ley = download_scjn_leyes_corpus("lamn")
historial = [s["codNota"] for s in ley["snapshots"] if s["codNota"]]   # oldest first

dest = reconstruct_legal_provisions(historial, "output", nombre_ley="LEY de Amnistía")
print(dest)   # output/ley-<first codNota>.md
```

Each note it needs is fetched through `legal_provisions` into the same
`outdir`, as `nota-{codNota}.md`; a note already there, from this law's own
previous run or another law's sharing the directory, is read back from disk
instead of fetched again.

## Why it is still here

The SCJN corpus became `legal_provisions`' default source, and that does not
retire this function. The corpus links 3,291 of its 3,724 `leyes` snapshots to
a `codNota`, only 526 of them pre-1999, and covers nothing outside federal
laws: replaying a law's own reform decrees remains the only route for
everything the corpus does not reach, and the independent cross-check on what
it does.

## `nombre_ley`

The catalogue's own `nombre` (`"LEY de Amnistía"`) scopes every note to the one
instrument among the several a single decree may touch. Pass it whenever a note
is shared with another law's history, which the release's per-law index does
not mark on its own (the reverse index does: `download_scjn_leyes_index` maps
one `codNota` to every law it reformed). Left out, a note is assumed to concern
only this law, which holds for most of them but silently mixes in another law's
articles for the rest.

## `source`

`source`, `min_confidence` and `keep_pages` are the same parameters
`legal_provisions` takes, forwarded to the call made for every note in the
history. The default here is `source="html"`, not `legal_provisions`' own
`"auto"`: the article merge was designed and checked against HTML-derived
Markdown, so a note missing `cadenaContenido` still fails by default. Passing
`source="image"` or `"pdf"` OCRs it instead of failing, but the merge's
behaviour on OCR output has not been validated; review the result before
trusting it.

## What the test establishes, and what it does not

`tests/test_leyes_44.py` checks the reconstruction against the SCJN's own
consolidated text at each law's most recent reform, over 42 real federal laws:
every federal law with two or three reforms, all published after 1999.
`scripts/regenera_fixtures_leyes.py` rewrites that ground truth from the
`scjn-leyes` release (see [Scripts](scripts.qmd)); the fixtures are the one
exception to "data is never committed", about 3 MB frozen so a regression test
of a replay algorithm does not change its answer because a law was reformed.

What is still checked, and is the point: the reconstruction replays the DOF's
own decrees, note by note, and nothing in that path reads the SCJN, so the
reconstruction and the fixture come from two different publishers of the same
law. What is not checked, anywhere: `legal_provisions` answers from the SCJN
corpus by default, and nothing compares that corpus against a source outside
itself. If the SCJN's text of a law is wrong, this suite passes.
